families.t: heaters, hot sheet, platens, trimming, vacuum and pressure, guards, interlocks, setup, cleaning and maintenance
f: HSE publishes practical safeguards for thermoforming machines.
Heaters and heated plastic sheet create burn hazards.
Moving platens, clamps and forming stations create crushing and trapping hazards.
Trimming and cutting equipment should be guarded against blade access.
Vacuum and pressure systems should be safely controlled and maintained.
Interlocks should prevent hazardous cycling when guards or access doors are open.
Setup, clearing, cleaning and maintenance need task-specific safe modes or isolation.
Damaged heaters, guards, interlocks or control devices should be reported and corrected before normal operation.
families.g: Thermoforming risk depends on heat, sheet and platen movement, cutters, vacuum or pressure, guarding and interlocks, setup access, isolation, maintenance and competence.

families.t: feed, screw and barrel, hot polymer, die, take-off, rollers, cutting, pressure, guarding, cleaning and isolation
f: HSE publishes practical safeguarding guidance for plastics extruder lines.
Feed openings and rotating screws should prevent access to dangerous movement.
Barrels, dies and molten polymer create severe burn hazards.
Take-off rollers, haul-offs and winding equipment create in-running nip hazards.
Cutters and downstream finishing equipment require suitable guarding.
Pressure and blockage-clearing tasks can release hot material unexpectedly.
Cleaning, die changes and maintenance should use secure isolation and controlled cooling.
Fume controls should be provided where heated polymers can produce irritating or harmful emissions.
families.g: Extrusion-line risk depends on screw and feed access, temperature and pressure, die and polymer condition, downstream nips and cutters, fume, isolation, maintenance and competence.

families.s: HSE plastics-processing fume prevention and control guidance
families.t: thermal degradation, irritant fume, process temperature, local exhaust ventilation, enclosure, maintenance, abnormal events and RPE
f: Any plastics fume can cause severe irritation to the eyes, nose and lungs.
Fume composition varies with polymer, additives, process temperature and degradation.
Process conditions should minimise overheating and decomposition.
Local exhaust ventilation should capture fume close to the source where needed.
Enclosure and automation can reduce operator exposure during normal processing.
Ventilation systems require examination, maintenance and performance checks.
Abnormal events such as burning, blocked dies or decomposition need planned response.
RPE can supplement but should not replace effective process and engineering controls.
families.g: Plastics-fume risk depends on polymer and additives, temperature, residence time, degradation, process enclosure, extraction, maintenance, abnormal events and respiratory protection.

families.s: HSE styrene exposure control in fibre-reinforced plastics manufacture
families.t: styrene vapour, contact moulding, WEL and STEL, resin selection, application method, ventilation, skin and eye protection and monitoring
f: Styrene vapour can irritate the nose, throat and lungs.
Symptoms can include difficulty concentrating, drowsiness, headache and nausea.
Styrene vapour and liquid splashes can irritate eyes and skin.
Employers should assess exposure and select controls that keep exposure below applicable limits.
Contact-moulding methods, resin formulation and application technique affect vapour release.
Local exhaust ventilation and work positioning should capture vapour near the source.
Gloves, eye protection and protective clothing should control residual splash and skin exposure.
Exposure monitoring and review are needed where control adequacy is uncertain or processes change.
families.g: Styrene risk depends on resin and styrene content, application method, surface area, temperature, ventilation, task duration, skin contact, monitoring and control maintenance.

families.s: HSE expandable-polystyrene pentane and cellular-plastic fire-risk guidance
families.t: pentane release, explosive atmospheres, zoning, ignition, static electricity, storage, smouldering, smoke, heaters and emergency response
f: Expandable polystyrene can release flammable pentane that must be considered in the DSEAR assessment.
Areas where pentane can accumulate should be assessed for explosive-atmosphere zoning.
Ignition sources, including electrical equipment and static discharge, should be controlled.
Ventilation should prevent dangerous accumulation of flammable vapour.
Storage layout and separation should limit fire spread.
Some cellular plastics can continue to smoulder after visible flames are extinguished.
Burning or smouldering plastics can produce thick smoke and toxic products.
Heaters, hot work, waste handling and emergency procedures should reflect the specific fire and explosion hazards.
families.g: Cellular-plastic fire risk depends on polymer and blowing agent, pentane release, ventilation and zoning, ignition and static control, inventory and storage, smouldering, smoke and emergency response.
